Summary
Rural income growth and poverty reduction influence each other through bidirectional channels, but the weight of cross-country and sector-specific evidence suggests a “growth-first” dynamic in many settings: sustained rural income growth reduces headcount poverty, especially when distribution is improved, while targeted poverty-reducing policies (cash transfers, infrastructure, pro-poor agriculture) accelerate poverty reduction and enable further growth by smoothing risk, expanding productive opportunities, and stimulating local demand. The causal priority depends on initial conditions, sectoral structure, and institutions; in some cases, inequality or structural change can reverse growth’s poverty impact, and in others neutrality or short-run bidirectional effects dominate. <cite id="15ac26c6-2">A rise in annual mean income growth reduces headcount poverty rates, but the poverty-reducing effect is altered when income growth is adjusted for initial spatial distributions of rural populations on degraded versus irrigated land, with higher shares on degraded land diminishing and higher shares on irrigated land enhancing the poverty-reducing impact of growth</cite> <cite id="15ac26c6-0">Scholars generally regard economic growth as a prerequisite for reducing rural poverty, yet high-quality, pro-poor growth with greater equity is needed, as “poverty-benefitting” growth and more equal distribution improve poverty outcomes</cite> <cite id="15ac26c6-3">In Indonesia, agricultural output growth is strongly linked to rural poverty reduction, whereas broad GDP growth was not inclusive, underscoring the role of sectoral and distributional inclusivity</cite> <cite id="120dabdb-0">Social protection can make vulnerable groups better equipped to share in growth opportunities, with mechanisms including risk smoothing, retention of productive assets, local demand multipliers, and improved labor supply responses</cite> <cite id="15ac26c6-4">Productivity growth in agriculture reduces poverty through higher farm incomes, employment generation, demand and food price effects benefiting net food consumers, real wage increases, and rural nonfarm multipliers</cite>.

Framing the question: levels, growth, and distribution
Poverty reduction can be measured as declines in headcount ratios or poverty gaps, while rural income growth reflects increases in per capita rural income or agricultural/GDP growth. Causality asks whether higher rural incomes precede and drive lower poverty (growth-first), or whether lower poverty enables higher incomes (poverty-reduction-first), or whether both reinforce each other (bidirectional). <cite id="15ac26c6-0">The literature clusters around three pillars: growth-driven poverty reduction, distribution/income-inequality dynamics, and the role of public policy and land/infrastructure reforms</cite>.

Macro and panel evidence on direction of causality
Cross-country panel analysis across 83 developing countries shows that increases in per capita income growth reliably reduce headcount poverty, with distributional adjustments altering the magnitude: higher shares of rural populations on degraded land dampen the effect, while higher shares on irrigated land amplify it. <cite id="15ac26c6-2">After adjusting income growth for initial spatial distributions, a 3.36% mean annual rural income growth translated into roughly 2.0–2.6% per-year poverty reduction for countries with high shares of rural populations on degraded land, illustrating how inclusive geography interacts with growth</cite>. This supports a growth-to-poverty effect, but with important distributional mediation. Related cross-country and regional studies converge on agriculture-led growth as a potent poverty-reduction engine. <cite id="15ac26c6-4">Evidence from the Green Revolution and empirical multi-country studies shows agriculture’s high returns to poverty reduction, with channels including direct farm income gains, rural employment, demand and food access effects, and spillovers to rural nonfarm activity</cite> <cite id="15ac26c6-3">In Indonesia, the decline in rural poverty is strongly linked to agricultural output growth and labor productivity, consistent with sectoral inclusivity</cite>.

However, growth-to-poverty causality is not universal. Causality frameworks reveal context-specific neutrality or bidirectional relations. <cite id="ebda1ae4-0">A Rwanda panel using ARDL bounds testing and Toda–Yamamoto Granger causality found no evidence that poverty reduction Granger-causes economic growth and vice versa in aggregate measures, implying a neutrality hypothesis for that period</cite>. <cite id="ebda1ae4-1">In Pakistan, Granger causality showed bi-directional short-run links between rural poverty and agricultural value added, with rural poverty also Granger-causing agricultural value-added, indicating feedbacks in the short run</cite>. <cite id="15ac26c6-2">Moreover, inequality can mask growth’s poverty-reducing effect, implying that growth alone may not lower poverty if incomes are concentrated</cite> <cite id="15ac26c6-0">Only “poverty-benefitting” high-quality growth and improved equity consistently translate into faster poverty reduction</cite>.

Mechanisms: why rural income growth reduces poverty
The agricultural sector transmits growth to poverty through multiple, empirically documented channels. <cite id="15ac26c6-4">A 10% growth in cereal yields cut rural poverty by over 53% in one study, and average yield growth of 2.5% in Latin America and the Caribbean was associated with rural poverty declines, illustrating large marginal poverty effects of productivity gains</cite>. <cite id="15ac26c6-4">Mechanisms include: higher farm real incomes, rural employment creation and absorption, induced demand for nonfarm goods and services, food price/availability effects benefiting net food consumers, rising real wages for unskilled labor, and rural social capital and nonfarm multiplier effects</cite>. Infrastructure provides a clean pathway linking productivity growth to poverty through lower production costs and better market access, while also enabling “trickle-down” via broader growth. <cite id="15ac26c6-1">Rural road investment stimulates productivity and incomes, with studies showing roads both reduce poverty directly and indirectly through growth, though risks of “hollow villages” can offset gains</cite>.

Policy shocks: poverty reduction that enables growth
Cash transfers and social protection demonstrate that reducing poverty first can unlock growth by mitigating risk and enabling productive investments. <cite id="120dabdb-0">Transfers can increase households’ willingness to take productive risks, retain assets under shocks, and spend locally, creating multipliers that benefit recipients and non-recipients</cite>. Large-scale evaluations in Latin America and sub-Saharan Africa show substantial and sustained reductions in monetary poverty and multidimensional deprivation. <cite id="120dabdb-1">Progresa/Oportunidades reduced the poverty gap by nearly 20% within a few years and improved child nutrition and schooling; Bolsa Família evidence points to entrepreneurship stimulation, consistent with poverty reduction enabling subsequent growth</cite> <cite id="120dabdb-3">Across sub-Saharan Africa, unconditional and conditional cash transfers have substantially reduced monetary poverty and generated local demand multipliers, with additional gains in household production, agricultural investments, schooling, and food security</cite> <cite id="120dabdb-4">A randomized rural Malawian scheme showed cash transfers raised consumption expenditures and altered risk-sharing, with evidence of crowding out some private gifts but not loans or remittances, highlighting complementary and sometimes competitive channels with existing support</cite>. Policy combinations matter: <cite id="120dabdb-0">evidence of positive links between social expenditure and growth suggests social protection can help vulnerable groups share in growth, with growth and social policy reinforcing each other</cite>.

Infrastructure and agrarian productivity as bidirectional levers
Infrastructure exemplifies bidirectional complementarities. <cite id="7d7cbd03-2">In China’s 2002–2017 panel, irrigation and drainage infrastructure directly reduced poverty, while rural transportation infrastructure both aggravated poverty via rural hollowing and indirectly reduced poverty by stimulating growth, with overall effects offsetting</cite> <cite id="7d7cbd03-4">Transportation investments promoted growth in tertiary industries (indirectly reducing poverty) but also induced rural depopulation (directly aggravating poverty), masking or reversing net effects depending on the balance of forces</cite>. This underscores that the order and co-evolution of policies and growth can shape poverty dynamics: <cite id="7d7cbd03-1">case evidence from Sri Lanka reports over 80% of households reporting higher incomes post-road development, with reduced cost-of-living and greater access to services, consistent with poverty reduction and local growth complementarities</cite>. Inclusive irrigation and rural connectivity can raise incomes and reduce vulnerability, with distributional safeguards important. <cite id="7d7cbd03-3">Studies in rural Laos and related evidence find irrigation raises household income and alleviates poverty, contributing to redressing inequality</cite>.

Counter-evidence and constraints
Neutruality and distributional reversals challenge a strict growth-first claim. <cite id="ebda1ae4-0">In Rwanda, no Granger causality between growth and poverty reduction over 1980–2016 suggests policy and structural factors rendered growth non-poor-benefitting during that period</cite>. Inequality can erode poverty declines even as per capita growth rises. <cite id="15ac26c6-2">Adjusting for initial spatial distributions, higher shares on degraded land diminish the poverty-reducing effect of growth, while higher shares on irrigated land enhance it</cite> <cite id="15ac26c6-0">and growing inequality is detrimental to future poverty reduction</cite>. Structural change and labor dynamics can reverse local growth benefits: <cite id="15ac26c6-1">transport-led urbanization can siphon off skilled and productive capital from rural areas, “hollowing” villages and increasing rural poverty despite aggregate growth</cite>. Sectoral exclusivity also matters: <cite id="15ac26c6-3">broad GDP growth may be non-inclusive, whereas agricultural sector growth is the reliable correlate of rural poverty reduction in Indonesia</cite>.

Resolving causal priority: a dynamic, context-dependent synthesis
Taken together, the balance of evidence supports a sequential, mutually reinforcing process rather than a single direction: rural income growth tends to reduce poverty when it is inclusive and geographically targeted, while poverty-reducing policies lower vulnerability and unlock productive investments, expanding the income base and enabling further growth. <cite id="15ac26c6-2">Rural income growth reduces headcount poverty, but the effect is mediated by distribution; growth is most effective when paired with equity-enhancing features</cite> <cite id="15ac26c6-4">and the agricultural channels from productivity to poverty are well documented</cite> <cite id="120dabdb-0">social protection broadens and stabilizes capacity to participate in markets, reinforcing growth</cite> <cite id="120dabdb-1">with demonstrated reductions in poverty and improvements in productive and human capital</cite>. Infrastructure exemplifies bidirectional complementarity: <cite id="7d7cbd03-2">it can directly lower poverty via reduced production costs and improved access, and indirectly via growth, but risks of rural hollowing create feedbacks where poverty reduction can also spur growth by retaining labor and assets</cite>.

Implications for policy and measurement
- Prioritize pro-poor, inclusive growth: <cite id="15ac26c6-0">equity-focused growth and “poverty-benefitting” quality of growth are critical for faster poverty reduction</cite> <cite id="15ac26c6-2">and spatially inclusive geography amplifies growth’s poverty impact</cite>.
- Combine safety nets with growth levers: <cite id="120dabdb-0">transfers stabilize risk and stimulate local demand, enabling households to seize growth opportunities</cite> <cite id="120dabdb-1">with documented poverty and human capital gains</cite>.
- Target agricultural productivity and irrigation with distributional safeguards: <cite id="15ac26c6-4">yields respond strongly to productivity improvements with large poverty effects</cite> <cite id="7d7cbd03-2">but irrigation reduces poverty directly; transport investments require measures to prevent rural hollowing</cite>.
- Diagnose context to avoid neutrality: <cite id="ebda1ae4-0">where policy and institutions neutralize growth, targeted interventions (e.g., in constraints, institutions) are needed to activate poverty-reducing effects</cite>.
- Decompose poverty change into growth and distribution: <cite id="15ac26c6-2">adjusting growth estimates for initial conditions clarifies the marginal poverty impact and highlights where redistribution is necessary</cite>.

Bottom line
In most rural settings, income growth reduces poverty when it is inclusive and geographically targeted; in turn, poverty reduction—via social protection and pro-poor agriculture—enables further income growth by expanding productive opportunities, stabilizing assets, and boosting local demand. The empirical record shows sequential leadership by growth, with poverty-reducing policies tipping the balance and infrastructure exemplifying bidirectional complementarities; however, in certain contexts inequality, structural change, or institutional constraints can reverse or neutralize these effects, making the causal priority context dependent rather than universal. <cite id="15ac26c6-2">Rural income growth reduces headcount poverty, with distributional and geographic mediation</cite> <cite id="15ac26c6-4">and well-documented agricultural productivity pathways to poverty reduction</cite> <cite id="120dabdb-0">social protection enables households to translate opportunities into higher incomes</cite> <cite id="15ac26c6-1">infrastructure acts both as a growth engine and a poverty lever, with caveats</cite> <cite id="ebda1ae4-0">and there are documented periods of neutrality requiring complementary reforms</cite>.</answer>

Title: The Impact of High-Standard Farmland Construction Policy on Rural Poverty in China
Snippet: Rural poverty is a complex phenomenon that is often the result of a variety of factors. The research on rural poverty is interdisciplinary and mainly focuses on three aspects. The first is economic growth and rural poverty reduction. Scholars usually regard economic growth as an important prerequisite for reducing rural poverty [19], and believe that both rural poor and non-poor groups can benefit from rural economic growth [20]. However, some scholars believe that economic growth alone does not necessarily alleviate poverty, and only "poverty-benefitting" high-quality economic growth can promote poverty reduction [21]. Furthermore, the degree of social equity is generally positively related to the poverty reduction effects of economic growth [22]. 

The second is income distribution and rural poverty reduction. Income inequalities will offset many of the poverty reduction effects caused by economic growth, which can at times even increase social poverty [23,24]. Ncube et al. [25] (2014) and Wan et al. [26] (2020) found that poverty reduction depends on more than the growth of average income and that income distribution plays a key role in promoting social welfare. Fang and Zhang [27] (2021) found that economic growth has contributed most to rural poverty reduction in all periods, but also that growing income inequality is detrimental to future poverty reduction. Therefore, future poverty reduction efforts should focus on pro-poor growth and income distribution equality. 

The third is the relationship between public policy and rural poverty reduction. Since the reform and opening up, China's achievements in poverty reduction have mainly been the result of its rapid economic growth, regional poverty reduction and development, social security policy, and preferential policy for agriculture and land systems [28]. Therefore, many scholars have investigated the relationship between public policy and poverty reduction [29]. Xu [30] (2016) found that the agricultural income of farmers will be affected by investment efficiency of rural public goods; the higher the investment efficiency, the higher the agricultural income of farmers. Some scholars also focus on land distribution policy [31,32]. Guo et al. [33] (2019) used survey data from rural households to explain the interactions between sustainable livelihood of rural household and agricultural land transfer. Peng et al. [34,35] found that land distribution can reduce poverty by reducing both agricultural production costs and farmers' vulnerability.

Title: Rural infrastructure and poverty in China
Snippet: Many empirical studies have suggested a positive role for rural infrastructure in allowing improvements to the quality of life of those living in poverty and alleviating poverty. Most of these studies highlight the impact of rural infrastructure on economic growth and thus indirectly on poverty, which is called a trickle-down effect [4][5][6][7][8][9]. The research by these authors illustrates that rural infrastructure such as rural transportation infrastructure can stimulate economic growth through gains in productivity, which in turn leads to increases in income and poverty alleviation. Sasmal, R., and Sasmal, J. (2016) and Chotia et al.,(2017) examine the connection between economic growth and poverty alleviation as well as how the two are connected to public infrastructure [10,11]. The results reveal that economic growth may drive poverty reduction, and infrastructure features largely in both growing the economy and reducing poverty. 

Some seminal works also pay attention to how rural infrastructure directly affects poverty. Most of the authors believe that rural infrastructure construction can directly reduce farmers' production costs and improve productivity, thereby increasing their income and reducing poverty [12,13]. Fan et al. (2005) reveal that investment in rural infrastructure can increase household income and pro-mote poverty reduction, with road infrastructure playing the most important role [6]. More recently, some scholars have pointed out that the improvement of rural infrastructure, especially rural transportation infrastructure, may promote urbanization. However, it may also lead to less productive capital and skilled labor in rural areas. In such "hollow villages", the rural poor may fall into greater poverty [14]. This increase in poverty may offset the poverty reduction effect of rural infrastructure, which we can call the masking effect, often used in mediation analysis in psychology [15][16][17]. Other studies also explore the relationship between irrigation and drainage infrastructure and rural income or rural poverty [18]. 

Overall, previous studies have emphasized the importance of rural infrastructure for poverty reduction. Most studies focus on how rural transportation infrastructure affects poverty reduction and usually find the negative relationship between rural transportation infrastructure and poverty. However, few literatures manage to figure out the mechanisms of how the irrigation and drainage infrastructure influence poverty. The specific poverty reduction mechanism behind the irrigation and drainage infrastructure needs to be further determined.

Title: Does Land Degradation Increase Poverty in Developing Countries?
Snippet: Our analysis of whether the 2000 distribution of rural populations in 83 developing countries on DAL and IAL influences changes in poverty rates over 2000-2012 for these countries focuses on four spatial distribution variables: 

• the share (%) of rural population located on all DAL (d 1 ); 

• the share (%) of rural population located on all remote DAL (d 2 ); 

• the share (%) of rural population located on all IAL (i 1 ); and 

• the share (%) of rural population located on all remote IAL (i 2 ). 

Table 3 summarizes the descriptive statistics for the key variables used in the poverty analysis for our sample of 83 countries (See also Table C in S1 File). 

For our sample of countries, we find no evidence that any of these four spatial distributions of the rural population in 2000 have a direct influence on poverty rates over 2000-2012. However, there is a statistically significant impact of these distributions through the poverty-reducing effects of income growth. 

As previous poverty-growth analyses have shown [18][19][20][21], a rise in annual mean income growth reduces headcount poverty rates. But we find that this poverty-reducing effect is altered significantly when we adjust income growth over 2000 to 2012 for each of the initial spatial population distributions d 1 , d 2 , i 1 and i 2 (Table 3). A higher share of the rural population on DAL (d 1 and d 2 ) diminishes the poverty-reducing impact of per capita income growth, whereas a higher share of the rural population on IAL (i 1 and i 2 ) enhances this poverty-reducing impact of growth. Consider an annual per capita income growth rate of 3.36%, which is the mean for the sample of 83 countries from 2000 to 2012 (Table 3). A country with a high share of rural population on degraded agricultural land d 1 , such as 48% (one-standard-deviation above the mean for all 83 countries), would expect to see a rate of poverty reduction of around 2.0 to 2.6% per year (Table 4).

Title: Does Agricultural Performance Contribute to Rural Poverty Reduction in Indonesia?
Snippet: In other words, to reduce rural poverty, the gap needs to be first addressed. Nguyen, Ngoc and Van der Weide (2010) in their study in Vietnam found that almost all regions experienced drastic poverty reduction from 1999 to 2006, the significant decrease happened on regions with a low gap, and in reverse, insignificant poverty reduction happened in regions with the high-income gap. 

If the Gini ratio were to be compared between the rural and urban Gini ratio, there is a tendency where the rural gap is lower than the urban gap. For instance, in 2017, the rural gap was 0.32, whereas the urban gap was 0.40. The income distribution gap in the rural area is relatively lower than the urban income distribution gap. However, the impact on poverty has the most reliable determinant. The government focus to solve the rural poverty problem should be started by improving the income distribution first. In order for land taxation (ownership) to be effective, it has to be progressively implemented. The target is to minimize land ownership in a particular group, which caused a gap in the rural area. 

Meanwhile, economic growth usually is an important contributor for poverty reduction in developing countries (Cervantes-Godoy and Dewbre, 2010;Cao, Wang and Wang, 2009;Sriyana, 2018), and several other countries have proven that growth significantly influences poverty reduction. Nevertheless, the calculated economic growth variable, in fact, has no significant influence to reduce rural poverty reduction in Indonesia. This reveals that economic growth in many regions is not inclusive. Adam Jr. (2004), argued that economic growth does not necessarily reduce poverty; it depends on how economic growth was defined. When growth is defined from GDP per capita, then its growth elasticity toward poverty is minimal; however, when growth is calculated from average income (consumption), its elasticity toward poverty will be higher. Sectorial growth based on jobs, as in the agricultural sector shows a significant result and has a negative correlation. If the agricultural sector constantly grows each year, it provides an effect on the reduction of rural poverty rate in Indonesia. The decrease of the rural poverty rate is strongly linked with the growth of agricultural output, which supported by labors' productivity (de Janvry and Sadoulet, 2010).

Title: Heterogeneous effects of improving technical efficiency on household multidimensional poverty: evidence from rural Ethiopia
Snippet: Several countries where agriculture is a major economic sector have introduced programs to ameliorate agrarian productivity because of its effective contribution to poverty reduction through better food security and higher farm inflows (FAO, 2017). However, people who depend on agriculture for their living are still generally much poorer than people who work in other sectors of the economy (Cervantes-Godoy and Dewbre, 2010). In the literature (Christiaensen et al., 2006;de Janvry and Sadoulet, 2010), growth in agriculture is much further responsible to poverty reduction than other sectors and renders advanced returns in terms of poverty reduction. The multiple routes through which growth in agrarian productivity can drive down poverty include: adding real income for the growers, employment generation, generating demand for non-agricultural goods, food price, and availability, thereby advantaging net food consumers, increasing real wages, thereby serving unskilled labor and building social capital, and rural non-farm multiplier effects (Irz et al., 2001;Minten and Barrett, 2008;Schneider and Gugerty, 2011;Ivanic and Martin, 2017). 

Growth in agriculture is also believed to bring a significant impact on poverty reduction, which comes not only from its direct poverty reduction effects but also from its potentially strong growth relation effects on the rest of the economy (de Janvry and Sadoulet, 2010). In addition, it has strong correlation with poverty reduction and large economy-wide multiplier 1 effects with other sectors in the rural economy (Suryahadi et al., 2006;Bezemer and Headey, 2008;Bekun and Akadiri, 2019), inferring that agrarian-led development strategies are sensational to achieve poverty reduction. The experience of the Green Revolution in Asia during the 1970s and 1980s also evidenced the role of agriculture as an instrument for poverty reduction and overall economic growth (Christiaensen et al., 2011). For illustration, the evidence documented by de Janvry and Sadoulet (2010) revealed that a 10% growth in cereal yields cut rural poverty by further than 53%. Also, the yield earnings in cereal in Latin America and the Caribbean that grew at an average annual rate of 2.5% were associated with a resultant decline in rural poverty.

Therefore, future poverty reduction efforts should focus on pro-poor growth and income distribution equality. 

The third is the relationship between public policy and rural poverty reduction. Since the reform and opening up, China's achievements in poverty reduction have mainly been the result of its rapid economic growth, regional poverty reduction and development, social security policy, and preferential policy for agriculture and land systems [28]. Therefore, many scholars have investigated the relationship between public policy and poverty reduction [29]. Xu [30] (2016) found that the agricultural income of farmers will be affected by investment efficiency of rural public goods; the higher the investment efficiency, the higher the agricultural income of farmers. Some scholars also focus on land distribution policy [31,32]. Guo et al. [33] (2019) used survey data from rural households to explain the interactions between sustainable livelihood of rural household and agricultural land transfer. Peng et al. [34,35] found that land distribution can reduce poverty by reducing both agricultural production costs and farmers' vulnerability.

documents.title: Rural infrastructure and poverty in China
documents.snippet:
Many empirical studies have suggested a positive role for rural infrastructure in allowing improvements to the quality of life of those living in poverty and alleviating poverty. Most of these studies highlight the impact of rural infrastructure on economic growth and thus indirectly on poverty, which is called a trickle-down effect [4][5][6][7][8][9]. The research by these authors illustrates that rural infrastructure such as rural transportation infrastructure can stimulate economic growth through gains in productivity, which in turn leads to increases in income and poverty alleviation. Sasmal, R., and Sasmal, J. (2016) and Chotia et al.,(2017) examine the connection between economic growth and poverty alleviation as well as how the two are connected to public infrastructure [10,11]. The results reveal that economic growth may drive poverty reduction, and infrastructure features largely in both growing the economy and reducing poverty. 

Some seminal works also pay attention to how rural infrastructure directly affects poverty. Most of the authors believe that rural infrastructure construction can directly reduce farmers' production costs and improve productivity, thereby increasing their income and reducing poverty [12,13]. Fan et al. (2005) reveal that investment in rural infrastructure can increase household income and pro-mote poverty reduction, with road infrastructure playing the most important role [6]. More recently, some scholars have pointed out that the improvement of rural infrastructure, especially rural transportation infrastructure, may promote urbanization. However, it may also lead to less productive capital and skilled labor in rural areas. In such "hollow villages", the rural poor may fall into greater poverty [14]. This increase in poverty may offset the poverty reduction effect of rural infrastructure, which we can call the masking effect, often used in mediation analysis in psychology [15][16][17]. Other studies also explore the relationship between irrigation and drainage infrastructure and rural income or rural poverty [18]. 

Overall, previous studies have emphasized the importance of rural infrastructure for poverty reduction. Most studies focus on how rural transportation infrastructure affects poverty reduction and usually find the negative relationship between rural transportation infrastructure and poverty. However, few literatures manage to figure out the mechanisms of how the irrigation and drainage infrastructure influence poverty. The specific poverty reduction mechanism behind the irrigation and drainage infrastructure needs to be further determined.

documents.title: Does Land Degradation Increase Poverty in Developing Countries?
documents.snippet:
Our analysis of whether the 2000 distribution of rural populations in 83 developing countries on DAL and IAL influences changes in poverty rates over 2000-2012 for these countries focuses on four spatial distribution variables: 

• the share (%) of rural population located on all DAL (d 1 ); 

• the share (%) of rural population located on all remote DAL (d 2 ); 

• the share (%) of rural population located on all IAL (i 1 ); and 

• the share (%) of rural population located on all remote IAL (i 2 ). 

Table 3 summarizes the descriptive statistics for the key variables used in the poverty analysis for our sample of 83 countries (See also Table C in S1 File). 

For our sample of countries, we find no evidence that any of these four spatial distributions of the rural population in 2000 have a direct influence on poverty rates over 2000-2012. However, there is a statistically significant impact of these distributions through the poverty-reducing effects of income growth. 

As previous poverty-growth analyses have shown [18][19][20][21], a rise in annual mean income growth reduces headcount poverty rates. But we find that this poverty-reducing effect is altered significantly when we adjust income growth over 2000 to 2012 for each of the initial spatial population distributions d 1 , d 2 , i 1 and i 2 (Table 3). A higher share of the rural population on DAL (d 1 and d 2 ) diminishes the poverty-reducing impact of per capita income growth, whereas a higher share of the rural population on IAL (i 1 and i 2 ) enhances this poverty-reducing impact of growth. Consider an annual per capita income growth rate of 3.36%, which is the mean for the sample of 83 countries from 2000 to 2012 (Table 3). A country with a high share of rural population on degraded agricultural land d 1 , such as 48% (one-standard-deviation above the mean for all 83 countries), would expect to see a rate of poverty reduction of around 2.0 to 2.6% per year (Table 4).

In other words, to reduce rural poverty, the gap needs to be first addressed. Nguyen, Ngoc and Van der Weide (2010) in their study in Vietnam found that almost all regions experienced drastic poverty reduction from 1999 to 2006, the significant decrease happened on regions with a low gap, and in reverse, insignificant poverty reduction happened in regions with the high-income gap. 

If the Gini ratio were to be compared between the rural and urban Gini ratio, there is a tendency where the rural gap is lower than the urban gap. For instance, in 2017, the rural gap was 0.32, whereas the urban gap was 0.40. The income distribution gap in the rural area is relatively lower than the urban income distribution gap. However, the impact on poverty has the most reliable determinant. The government focus to solve the rural poverty problem should be started by improving the income distribution first. In order for land taxation (ownership) to be effective, it has to be progressively implemented. The target is to minimize land ownership in a particular group, which caused a gap in the rural area. 

Meanwhile, economic growth usually is an important contributor for poverty reduction in developing countries (Cervantes-Godoy and Dewbre, 2010;Cao, Wang and Wang, 2009;Sriyana, 2018), and several other countries have proven that growth significantly influences poverty reduction. Nevertheless, the calculated economic growth variable, in fact, has no significant influence to reduce rural poverty reduction in Indonesia. This reveals that economic growth in many regions is not inclusive. Adam Jr. (2004), argued that economic growth does not necessarily reduce poverty; it depends on how economic growth was defined. When growth is defined from GDP per capita, then its growth elasticity toward poverty is minimal; however, when growth is calculated from average income (consumption), its elasticity toward poverty will be higher. Sectorial growth based on jobs, as in the agricultural sector shows a significant result and has a negative correlation. If the agricultural sector constantly grows each year, it provides an effect on the reduction of rural poverty rate in Indonesia. The decrease of the rural poverty rate is strongly linked with the growth of agricultural output, which supported by labors' productivity (de Janvry and Sadoulet, 2010).

documents.title: Heterogeneous effects of improving technical efficiency on household multidimensional poverty: evidence from rural Ethiopia
documents.snippet:
Several countries where agriculture is a major economic sector have introduced programs to ameliorate agrarian productivity because of its effective contribution to poverty reduction through better food security and higher farm inflows (FAO, 2017). However, people who depend on agriculture for their living are still generally much poorer than people who work in other sectors of the economy (Cervantes-Godoy and Dewbre, 2010). In the literature (Christiaensen et al., 2006;de Janvry and Sadoulet, 2010), growth in agriculture is much further responsible to poverty reduction than other sectors and renders advanced returns in terms of poverty reduction. The multiple routes through which growth in agrarian productivity can drive down poverty include: adding real income for the growers, employment generation, generating demand for non-agricultural goods, food price, and availability, thereby advantaging net food consumers, increasing real wages, thereby serving unskilled labor and building social capital, and rural non-farm multiplier effects (Irz et al., 2001;Minten and Barrett, 2008;Schneider and Gugerty, 2011;Ivanic and Martin, 2017). 

Growth in agriculture is also believed to bring a significant impact on poverty reduction, which comes not only from its direct poverty reduction effects but also from its potentially strong growth relation effects on the rest of the economy (de Janvry and Sadoulet, 2010). In addition, it has strong correlation with poverty reduction and large economy-wide multiplier 1 effects with other sectors in the rural economy (Suryahadi et al., 2006;Bezemer and Headey, 2008;Bekun and Akadiri, 2019), inferring that agrarian-led development strategies are sensational to achieve poverty reduction. The experience of the Green Revolution in Asia during the 1970s and 1980s also evidenced the role of agriculture as an instrument for poverty reduction and overall economic growth (Christiaensen et al., 2011). For illustration, the evidence documented by de Janvry and Sadoulet (2010) revealed that a 10% growth in cereal yields cut rural poverty by further than 53%. Also, the yield earnings in cereal in Latin America and the Caribbean that grew at an average annual rate of 2.5% were associated with a resultant decline in rural poverty.

Title: Does Economic Growth Contribute to Poverty Reduction? An Empirical Analysis Evidence from Rwanda
Snippet: This study empirically analyzes whether economic growth contributed to poverty reduction in Rwanda over the period of 1980-2016. The study applied the Autoregressive - Distribution Lag bounds approach to testing for cointegration, as well Toda and Yamamoto (TY) Granger causality was used in testing for the directional causality among the variables in the study. The Autoregressive - Distribution Lag bounds test results confirm the cointegration between Household final consumption expenditure, Arable land growth rate (hectares), Gross capital formation growth rate (% of GDP), Government final consumption expenditure growth rate (% of GDP) and Service value-added growth rate, when the Household final consumption expenditure, Arable land growth rate and Gross capital formation growth rate are used as dependent variable. Additional, the results from Toda and Yamamoto Granger causality confirms a no evidence of causality association linking the poverty reduction to economic growth and vice versa while considering log Household final consumption expenditure and Arable land growth rate as dependent variables. This means that the neutrality hypothesis grips for Rwanda in the period covered by the study. Furthermore, the study finds out a proof of unidirectional causality running from Gross capital formation growth rate to government final consumption expenditure growth rate, as well as unidirectional causality running from Arable land growth rate to Government final consumption expenditure growth rate and Service value-added growth to Government final consumption expenditure growth rate. The study findings suggested that the government should adopt policy?s objective which is focusing on poverty reduction and economic growth.

Therefore, the outcomes show a short-term association between the agricultural value-added and rural poverty, agricultural labor force and rural poverty, and government final consumption expenditure and the rural poverty.

Title: The Nexus between Finance, Growth and Poverty in India: The Cointegration and Causality Approach1
Snippet: The paper examines the causal nexus between financial development, economic growth and poverty reduction in India during 1951-2008. The empirical analysis is based on cointegration and causality test. The cointegration test finds the presence of long run equilibrium relationship between financial development, economic growth and poverty reduction. The Granger causality test at the end confirms the presence of unidirectional causality from poverty reduction to economic growth, economic growth to finance development, financial development to poverty reduction and economic growth to poverty reduction. It also finds no causality between finance development and economic growth, and poverty reduction and finance development. The paper suggests that economic growth is considered as the policy variable to accelerate finance development and both could be used as the policy variable to reduce poverty in the economy.

Title: An inquiry into the nexus between energy poverty and income inequality in the light of global evidence
Snippet: Econometrically, the assumption of the system equation in Eq. [7] is that energy poverty and income inequality have a mutual linkage or two-way causal nexus. To prove this point, the study first employs the Granger causality test for panel data, following the approach developed by Dumitrescu and Hurlin (2012). In so doing, it examines the causality between each proxy of energy poverty and income inequality. In fact, while the validity of the Granger causality test has been criticised in the econometrics literature (see Haufe, Nikulin et al. (2012)), it is used to provide a piece of additional econometric evidence for our hypothesis on the mutual nexus between energy poverty and income inequality. The results of panel Granger causality are presented in Table 3, showing statistical significance causal impact of energy poverty and income inequality on each other, excluding insignificant statistics in the causality of EP1 to both II1 and II2, respectively. The results firstly imply that there are bidirectional causalities between energy poverty and income inequality in most aspects, except the uni-directional causality from income inequality to the use of clean fuels and technologies for cooking (EP1). This is an interesting finding, that access to electricity (total, rural area, urban area) or electricity consumption has mutual causality with income inequality, while there is only one-directional causality from the use of clean fuels and technologies for cooking on income inequality, but the reverse causality is not statistically signifiance. (Dumitrescu & Hurlin (2012)): H0: X does not Granger-cause Y; H1: X does Granger-cause Y for at least one panelvar (country). *** is significant at 1%. 

The results in Table 3 provide statistical evidence supporting the hypothesis and the estimation of the system equation in Eq. [7]. In estimating structural equations with mutual linkages between dependent variables, the econometrics literature suggests the two-stage least squares (2SLS) estimate as appropriate for the analysis of structural equation (James andSingh 1978, Angrist andImbens 1995).

Title: When growth is not enough: Do government transfers moderate the effect of economic growth on absolute and relative child poverty?
Snippet: These approaches reviewed above suggest that social protection contributes to poverty reduction directly through redistribution.But, cash transfers could additionally have indirect effects on the incomes of poor households by strengthening their capacities to earn income from the market.At societal level, there is now increasing evidence of a positive link between some types of social expenditure and economic growth (e.g.Cammeraat, 2020), potentially with particular relevance for the welfare of low-income households.Globally, growing attention is paid to the potential multiplier effects of cash transfers (Gassmann et al., 2023).Social protection, including cash transfers, can accordingly make vulnerable groups better equipped to share in the opportunities associated with increased economic activity.

A number of mechanisms linking transfers to higher productivity among poor households, also in the shorter run, are highlighted in the literature (Alderman and Yemtsov, 2012;Barrientos, 2012).First, because poverty is associated with risk aversion, security provided through the receipt of a regular cash transfer could encourage poor people to take certain risks, such as searching for more productive employment opportunities or making different kinds of productive investments.Second, cash transfers can enable poor people to employ more beneficial coping strategies, for example, by retaining productive assets in face of external shocks to the household's economy.Third, as the poor tend to spend locally, cash transfers are likely to stimulate demand for goods and services, promoting growth in local economies, thereby benefitting also non-recipients (see, for example, Barrientos and Malerba, 2020).

Transfer schemes could also have other consequences for labour markets, such as increasing reservation wages and thus potentially raise earnings for low-paid workers.The sceptic view that government transfers could generate more poverty by depressing labour supply through the lowering of work incentives, has moreover been mostly dispelled by research from developing countries (Barrientos and Malerba, 2020;Bastagli et al., 2019;Fiszbein and Schady, 2009).In fact, some studies point to increased labour market participation as transfers are used to cover cost for job searching and migration.However, a lack of economic opportunities could hamper the positive effects of a greater productive capacity of households (Barrientos, 2012), pointing to the combination of growth and social policy as a key factor.

Title: Impact of Livelihood Empowerment against Poverty Programme in Ghana: The Case of Wa West District
Snippet: There exists considerable evidence of the impact of cash transfers programmes. Some of the benefits of cash transfer include poverty alleviation, improvement in health, high educational and nutritional outcomes, growth in the economy, empowerment, especially for women, and a general social cohesion. Poverty alleviation and reduction in vulnerability however, remain the primary objectives of cash transfer programmes. This is because such transfers are expected to positively impact on the productive strategies and livelihoods of poor people. In the long term, the effects of cash transfer as evidence suggests, can help break the intergenerational transmission of poverty (Devereux & Coll-Black, 2007). A lot of the evidence on the long term effects of cash transfer derives from the literature of one of the most evaluated programmes, Mexico's Progresa, later renamed Oportunidades). Evidence from these research studies indicate that partaking in the programme results in improvements in the productive capacity of poor households in the long term. The poverty gap, as a result of this cash transfer, reduced by 30% among beneficiaries after two years of operation; raised the height-for-age of beneficiary children by 1 cm after two years compared with a control group; and is also projected to raise the years of schooling among beneficiary children completing the education cycle by close to one additional year. The Bolsa Família in Brazil also generated some understanding on the long term effects, including the prospect of cash transfers stimulating entrepreneurship amongst recipients (Fiszbein et al., 2009). 

Evidence also abounds, that cash transfers have curtailed the incidence of poverty and its severity (i.e. the poverty gap) amongst most evaluated middle income country programmes. Studies across countries have consistently demonstrated evidence of positive impacts as per capita consumption has increased. Household data analysis shows that the marginal effect of non-contributory pension receipt within the household is to reduce the probability of poverty by 18% in Brazil and 12.5% in South Africa (Barrientos, 2005). Micro simulation modeling with latest household survey data approximates that the Progresa/ Oportunidades programme in Mexico has reduced the poverty gap by almost 20%, from 8.5 to 6.8 (Fiszbein et al., 2009).

Title: Can cash transfers reduce child labor?
Snippet: Social protection policies such as cash transfers seem to be an obvious way to reduce child labor. Cash transfers aim to relieve household economic hardship by providing income support. By easing the economic vulnerability of households, cash transfers can remove some of the reasons why children work. Cash transfer benefits are often coupled with incentives for behavioral change, as in the case of conditional cash transfers that include conditions for children's education or health care. 

A small change in the budget constraint might not be effective in changing the bahvior of very poor households. Moreover, cash transfers can have complex effects on household behavior that go beyond easing budget constraints. For example, if cash transfers change the relative prices of children's time use (in work and schooling), that may affect a household's decision to send a child to school. School attendance requires the commitment of a certain amount of a child's time and incurs some fixed costs, which are likely to change the financial constraints facing the household. Also, the household might use part of the transfer for investments in productive assets instrumental to farming or small business activities, such as fertilizer, plows, or sewing machines, which can make it more profitable for children to work. Both of these mechanisms make the effect of cash transfer programs on child labor uncertain. This article discusses some of the potential benefits and limitations of cash transfers for vulnerable households, drawing on extensive evidence from impact evaluations. While this does not exhaust the evidence on this topic, focusing on impact evaluations means relying on statistically solid information generated by actual cash transfer programs. Also, there are limits to what cash transfers and, more generally, social protection programs can do to reduce child labor. Access to and the quality of education, returns to education, and access to good jobs after graduation are a few of the variables that also shape household decisions affecting children's work.

Snippet: While there have been some studies of crowding out effects of social cash transfers programs in Latin America, very few studies have been done in Sub-Saharan Africa and even fewer are based on a randomized experiment. Title: Rural infrastructure and poverty in China
Snippet: Many empirical studies have suggested a positive role for rural infrastructure in allowing improvements to the quality of life of those living in poverty and alleviating poverty. Most of these studies highlight the impact of rural infrastructure on economic growth and thus indirectly on poverty, which is called a trickle-down effect [4][5][6][7][8][9]. The research by these authors illustrates that rural infrastructure such as rural transportation infrastructure can stimulate economic growth through gains in productivity, which in turn leads to increases in income and poverty alleviation. Sasmal, R., and Sasmal, J. (2016) and Chotia et al.,(2017) examine the connection between economic growth and poverty alleviation as well as how the two are connected to public infrastructure [10,11]. The results reveal that economic growth may drive poverty reduction, and infrastructure features largely in both growing the economy and reducing poverty. 

Some seminal works also pay attention to how rural infrastructure directly affects poverty. Most of the authors believe that rural infrastructure construction can directly reduce farmers' production costs and improve productivity, thereby increasing their income and reducing poverty [12,13]. Fan et al. (2005) reveal that investment in rural infrastructure can increase household income and pro-mote poverty reduction, with road infrastructure playing the most important role [6]. More recently, some scholars have pointed out that the improvement of rural infrastructure, especially rural transportation infrastructure, may promote urbanization. However, it may also lead to less productive capital and skilled labor in rural areas. In such "hollow villages", the rural poor may fall into greater poverty [14]. This increase in poverty may offset the poverty reduction effect of rural infrastructure, which we can call the masking effect, often used in mediation analysis in psychology [15][16][17]. Other studies also explore the relationship between irrigation and drainage infrastructure and rural income or rural poverty [18]. 

Overall, previous studies have emphasized the importance of rural infrastructure for poverty reduction. Most studies focus on how rural transportation infrastructure affects poverty reduction and usually find the negative relationship between rural transportation infrastructure and poverty. However, few literatures manage to figure out the mechanisms of how the irrigation and drainage infrastructure influence poverty. The specific poverty reduction mechanism behind the irrigation and drainage infrastructure needs to be further determined.

Title: Examining the Influence of Rural Road Network Development on Livelihood - A Case Study on Kilinochchi District
Snippet: A more excellent supply and mix of transport networks and an improved movement of goods and services have been noted. The studied project sites are predominantly farming populations and, thus, are vulnerable to natural shocks or product price fluctuations. Therefore, their capacity to diversify into other sources of income is necessary to minimise poverty. Of course, those who are more comfortable and have savings can make the maximum use of the possibilities improved roads can offer. The multidimensional concept of poverty used in the study assumes that the reduction of poverty will benefit from improvements in sources of income and greater exposure to social services. Income diversification will mitigate exposure to external shocks. Improving rural roads will create new income-generating opportunities and increase access to critical services. This chapter provides data from case research on improvements in sources of income and healthcare and how these changes apply to various social classes. 

Figure 14 describes the ratings for the increment in the household income of the village after the road development. 84% of the respondents proved that their income had increased more than the previous. 

The reduction in the cost of living in the village after the road development is depicted in Figure 15. Approximately 10% of respondents indicated that their poverty has only slightly decreased their cost of living. Here, a reduction in the cost of living increased means the cost of living has reduced. 

Numerous authors have addressed the link between poverty reduction and the provision of rural infrastructure from a macro perspective (Ahmed Donovan, 1992;Chongvilaivan et al., 2016;Corral Reardon, 2001;Iimi et al., 2015;Shantha, 2019). Most of them point to solid ties between investment in rural infrastructure, development in agriculture, and poverty reduction. These studies are focused on evidence from countries worldwide, such as Indonesia, Brazil, and Malaysia, where long periods of economic growth and a drastic decline in rural poverty have accompanied a significant increase in rural infrastructure. Although the causal relation is not well known, they propose that this may have resulted as a result of the effect of improvements in infrastructure on the growth in agricultural production and the development of new employment opportunities.

Title: Rural infrastructure and poverty in China
Snippet: The study develops a theoretical framework of how irrigation and drainage infrastructure and rural transportation infrastructure influence poverty. Using panel data on 31 provinces in China from 2002 to 2017, this paper estimates basic and continuous difference-in-differences (DID) models to investigate the preliminary impact of irrigation and drainage infrastructure and rural transportation infrastructure on poverty and further explores the influence mechanisms of these rural infrastructures on poverty by using the mediating effect model. The results show that irrigation and drainage facilities infrastructure can directly reduce poverty. On the one hand, rural transportation infrastructure directly leads to rural hollowing out and aggravates rural poverty; on the other hand, it indirectly promotes poverty reduction by stimulating economic growth. Overall, the positive and negative effects of rural transportation infrastructure on poverty offset each other.

Title: Public Investment on Irrigation and Poverty Alleviation in Rural Laos
Snippet: Michael et al. (2003) examined the effect of irrigation on the alleviation of poverty in India. They conducted descriptive and qualitative analysis to understand the effect of irrigation on the environment due to building a dam. The results of their study contributed to the economic growth, which was insignificant compared to that of the irrigation in the 1970's. The study indicated the irrigation system presents a vital component in the agriculture production in a major effort to alleviate poverty. Huang et al. (2002) examined the impact of irrigation on income, poverty and distribution of income in rural regions by using the information gathered in rural areas in 2000. They used descriptive analysis to explain the relationship between irrigation and income and irrigation and poverty. The term "decomposed" to denote the source of income and the people with and without access to irrigation included in the study on the effect of irrigation on income distribution and inequality. The study demonstrated irrigation had a direct impact on income and poverty and contributed to redressing inequality as well. Bose et al. (2007) assessed the effect of the outcome of government expenditure on the economic growth of some 30 developing countries between the period of 1970-1980 using the "endogeneity test" and three-stage least squares (3SLS). Although the study hinted at some significant difference in government expenditure between developed and developing countries, result of the study, in contrast, revealed the government expenditure on transportation, communication and defense was insignificant compared to that on education regarding the long-term economic growth in the developing countries. 

This paper sought to answer the question, "what is the impact of infrastructural investments in irrigation on rural household income, which leads to poverty alleviation in rural Laos?" and, more precisely, "what are the mechanisms that can be used to influence rural household income?" The findings of this study can contribute to evaluating the impact of infrastructure investments, particularly irrigation, on poverty alleviation by bringing in new empirical evidence and can be used as a source of information for policymakers in making an appropriate policy for poverty eradication in the future.

Title: Rural infrastructure and poverty in China
Snippet: This study develops a theoretical framework of how irrigation and drainage infrastructure and rural transportation infrastructure influence poverty. Along with provincial panel data on China from 2002 to 2017, this paper uses a basic DID model to examine how investment policy on rural infrastructure influences poverty in rural China. Then a continuous DID model is used to investigate how two of the most important rural infrastructures, irrigation and drainage infrastructure and rural transportation infrastructure, influence rural poverty in China. 

Instrumental variable estimation and a change in the independent variable are used to enhance the robustness of the results. In addition, the mediating effect model is used to investigate the influence mechanisms of irrigation and drainage infrastructure and rural transportation infrastructure on rural poverty in China. Most of these studies highlight the impact of rural infrastructure on economic growth and thus indirectly on poverty, which is called a trickle-down effect [4][5][6][7][8][9]. (2016) and Chotia et al.,(2017) examine the connection between economic growth and poverty alleviation as well as how the two are connected to public infrastructure [10,11]. The results reveal that economic growth may drive poverty reduction, and infrastructure features largely in both growing the economy and reducing poverty. 

Some seminal works also pay attention to how rural infrastructure directly affects poverty. Most of the authors believe that rural infrastructure construction can directly reduce farmers' production costs and improve productivity, thereby increasing their income and reducing poverty [12,13]. Fan et al. (2005) reveal that investment in rural infrastructure can increase household income and pro-mote poverty reduction, with road infrastructure playing the most important role [6]. More recently, some scholars have pointed out that the improvement of rural infrastructure, especially rural transportation infrastructure, may promote urbanization. However, it may also lead to less productive capital and skilled labor in rural areas. In such "hollow villages", the rural poor may fall into greater poverty [14]. This increase in poverty may offset the poverty reduction effect of rural infrastructure, which we can call the masking effect, often used in mediation analysis in psychology [15][16][17]. Other studies also explore the relationship between irrigation and drainage infrastructure and rural income or rural poverty [18].

Most studies focus on how rural transportation infrastructure affects poverty reduction and usually find the negative relationship between rural transportation infrastructure and poverty. The specific poverty reduction mechanism behind the irrigation and drainage infrastructure needs to be further determined.

(2007) assessed the effect of the outcome of government expenditure on the economic growth of some 30 developing countries between the period of 1970-1980 using the "endogeneity test" and three-stage least squares (3SLS). Although the study hinted at some significant difference in government expenditure between developed and developing countries, result of the study, in contrast, revealed the government expenditure on transportation, communication and defense was insignificant compared to that on education regarding the long-term economic growth in the developing countries. 

This paper sought to answer the question, "what is the impact of infrastructural investments in irrigation on rural household income, which leads to poverty alleviation in rural Laos?" and, more precisely, "what are the mechanisms that can be used to influence rural household income?" The findings of this study can contribute to evaluating the impact of infrastructure investments, particularly irrigation, on poverty alleviation by bringing in new empirical evidence and can be used as a source of information for policymakers in making an appropriate policy for poverty eradication in the future.

- Fastest measurable impacts in rural poverty reduction are typically delivered by cash-based social protection (contingent or recurrent transfers) and rural electrification, with large and statistically credible gains in household consumption and poverty within 1–2 years; rural feeder roads and agriculture-oriented subsidies also show rapid effects but with more heterogeneity across settings. <cite id="6a262056-0">There is substantial evidence that cash transfer schemes substantially reduce monetary poverty in sub-Saharan Africa and generate local multiplier effects</cite> <cite id="6a262056-4">and that well-evaluated programs like Mexico’s Progresa reduced the poverty gap by around 30% after two years and increased child height-for-age by about 1 cm</cite>. <cite id="ec5b5395-1">In India, access to electricity increased monthly per capita consumption by over 50% in rural households and raised the probability of transitioning out of poverty by 22%, with effects detectable within a year</cite> <cite id="ec5b5395-3">while reliable supply magnified income gains versus mere connection</cite>. <cite id="e8844cf6-2">Rural roads can be more pro-poor than urban/tarmac roads and may reduce poverty up to three times per unit investment, acting quickly via lower transport costs and market access</cite>. <cite id="e8844cf6-1">Agriculture-focused subsidy diversion simulations show sizable poverty reductions—greater in rural than urban areas—indicating fast income effects from enabling production and marketing</cite>.

What the evidence shows by strategy

1) Cash transfers and social protection platforms
- Mechanism and speed: <cite id="6a262056-0">Cash transfers protect and smooth consumption, with documented reductions in monetary poverty and complementary effects on agricultural investment and schooling</cite>. <cite id="6a262056-4">In Progresa, the poverty gap fell by 30% after two years; household-level analyses show non-contributory pension receipt reduces poverty probability by 12.5% in South Africa and ~18% in Brazil</cite>. <cite id="6a262056-3">Across Sub-Saharan Africa, transfers reduce hunger and poverty quickly, but sustained exit often requires adequate transfer size, regularity, and predictability to translate into productive investments</cite>. 
- Rural context: <cite id="6a262056-1">In Indonesian rural villages, Village Cash Transfers increased per capita consumption, though distributional targeting was imperfect; impacts were larger for middle-to-upper quantiles and smaller (or negative) for the poorest without adjustments</cite>. <cite id="6a262056-3">Program design—adequacy, predictability, and timing aligned with agricultural cycles—determines how quickly transfers translate into livelihood improvements</cite>. 
- Why fast: Cash directly increases liquidity among the poorest, enabling immediate purchases and smoothing, with multipliers in local markets; conditionality or work requirements can accelerate human capital and asset formation over 1–3 years. <cite id="6a262056-0">Evidence from SSA shows cash transfers substantially reduce monetary poverty with local economic multipliers</cite> <cite id="6a262056-4">and early gains in nutrition and schooling within two years</cite>.

2) Rural electrification
- Mechanism and speed: <cite id="ec5b5395-1">Access raises monthly per capita consumption expenditure by 53% in rural areas (and 37% in urban poor), with an additional hour of electricity yielding ~3–4% higher consumption; the probability of transitioning out of poverty rises by 22% with access</cite>. <cite id="ec5b5395-3">Reliability is crucial: reliable 24-hour supply yields 17% income gains versus 11% with only connection, and non-farm income rises by 28% with reliable power</cite>. 
- Early versus medium-term: <cite id="ec5b5395-4">In western Indonesia, electrification reduced the rural poverty rate significantly at a two-period lag, with short-run effects concentrated on non-food consumption and welfare improvements</cite>. <cite id="ec5b5395-0">Studies also find shifts from food to non-food spending and greater ownership of appliances in the first years as households smooth demand</cite>. 
- Why fast: Power enables round-the-clock work, processing, and services; it increases market participation and income-generating activities, especially when supply is reliable and affordable. <cite id="ec5b5395-3">Per additional outage hour, per capita income falls by 0.5% and reliable supply multiplies gains over connection alone</cite>. 
- Caveat: <cite id="ec5b5395-1">Effects vary by baseline access and hours; electrification alone without sufficient hours delivers smaller benefits, and poorest households show gains at observed margins</cite>.

3) Rural roads and transport last-mile
- Mechanism and speed: <cite id="e8844cf6-2">Feeder rural roads directly support the poorest in agriculture-dependent areas by cutting transport costs to markets and services; recent reviews argue rural roads can reduce poverty up to three times more per dollar than higher-standard roads and act quickly as “pro-poor” last-mile infrastructure</cite>. <cite id="e8844cf6-2">Evidence from Sri Lanka, India, and Ghana shows rural roads comprise large shares of networks and disproportionately benefit those missing out from major infrastructure</cite>. 
- Why fast: Lower transport costs and improved access raise incomes through reduced trading costs and improved land/produce marketing within 1–3 years, especially where markets are distant. <cite id="e8844cf6-2">Analyses emphasize last-mile mobility as a lever for rapid welfare gains</cite>.

4) Agriculture-oriented subsidies and asset/technology support
- Mechanism and speed: <cite id="e8844cf6-1">Simulations that divert fuel/inputs subsidies toward non-food crops raise rural household incomes enough to lift many above the poverty line within a year, with larger rural impacts than urban</cite>. <cite id="6a262056-3">Where transfers or input subsidies are large, predictable, and aligned with agricultural cycles, households increase input purchases and non-farm business opportunities within 1–2 years, but effects are mixed and context-dependent</cite>. 
- Caveats for speed: <cite id="6a262056-3">Productive impacts require sufficient adequacy and liquidity; without complementary extension, markets, or credit, gains can be lumpy or slow</cite>. <cite id="ec5b5395-0">Some studies find no significant income or poverty effects from electrification in certain contexts, underscoring the need for complementary reforms</cite>. 

5) Public works and social protection platforms
- Mechanism and speed: <cite id="6a262056-0">Cash-based social protection programs deliver quick consumption smoothing and often spur local economic activity and agricultural investments</cite>. <cite id="6a262056-3">Programs in Lesotho and Zambia increased agricultural input purchases and non-farm business opportunities within 1–2 years when transfers were sufficiently large and predictable</cite>. Platforms that combine transfers, training, and assets can accelerate impacts by combining liquidity with productive guidance. 
- Boundary: <cite id="6a262056-3">Without adequate adequacy and predictability, transfers become lumpy and fail to sustainably move households out of poverty</cite>.

6) Rural microfinance and markets
- Mechanism and speed: <cite id="6a262056-4">Evidence on microfinance’s anti-poverty effects is mixed; while credit can support entrepreneurship, robust long-run poverty reduction is less clearly demonstrated than with cash transfers, and effects can be slower without broader market and risk-sharing infrastructure</cite>. 
- Caveat: <cite id="6a262056-3">Where liquidity constraints dominate, cash is more effective at smoothing and enabling early income gains than loans that require collateral or market linkages</cite>.

Comparative speed: What differentiates the winners
- Liquidity and adequacy: <cite id="6a262056-3">Transfers that are large enough, regular, predictable, and timed around agricultural cycles translate faster into consumption smoothing and productive investments</cite>. <cite id="6a262056-4">Progresa’s early gains in poverty gap (two years), nutrition, and education illustrate how cash can rapidly reduce monetary poverty and build human capital</cite>. 
- Last-mile relief of constraints: <cite id="e8844cf6-2">Rural roads and electrification quickly raise welfare by lowering transport and time costs, enabling round-the-clock work, and expanding services/markets</cite>. <cite id="ec5b5395-3">Reliability multiplies income gains, shortening the time path to poverty reduction</cite>. 
- Agricultural targeting: <cite id="e8844cf6-1">Subsidy diversion toward rural non-food crops produced sizable poverty cuts within a year, especially where rural access structures make adoption easier</cite>. 
- Targeting and distribution: <cite id="6a262056-1">If transfers are poorly targeted to the poorest, early gains may miss the ultra-poor; adjustments to increase recipients and deepen support among the poorest accelerate impact</cite>.

Evidence-backed speed rankings (roughly, by typical time to measurable poverty impact in rural areas)
1) Cash transfers/social protection (contingent/unconditional): <cite id="6a262056-0">Reduce monetary poverty quickly in SSA and Latin America</cite> <cite id="6a262056-4">with documented poverty-gap declines within two years and improvements in food security and schooling</cite>. 
2) Rural electrification (especially with reliable supply): <cite id="ec5b5395-1">Within one year, access and additional hours raise consumption and poverty-transition probabilities</cite> <cite id="ec5b5395-3">and reliable power substantially amplifies income effects</cite>. 
3) Rural roads/last-mile transport: <cite id="e8844cf6-2">Within 1–3 years, poverty reductions per dollar can be larger for rural feeder roads due to direct benefits to poor, agriculture-dependent households</cite>. 
4) Agriculture-oriented subsidies/asset transfers (conditional on design): <cite id="e8844cf6-1">Rural poverty declines materially when subsidies are redirected to non-food crops</cite> <cite id="6a262056-3">but impacts vary; productivity multipliers often emerge over 1–3 years if adequate and predictable</cite>. 
5) Public works and microfinance: <cite id="6a262056-3">Work and asset programs can accelerate early income via employment and investment</cite> <cite id="6a262056-4">but entrepreneurship effects are slower and more heterogeneous; microfinance alone is mixed</cite>.

Why the ranking differs across studies
- Measurement horizons and metrics: <cite id="ec5b5395-4">Electrification’s poverty effects may materialize after two years as usage and income-generating activities ramp</cite> <cite id="6a262056-3">while transfers show immediate consumption and poverty-gap changes</cite>. 
- Implementation quality: <cite id="6a262056-1">Targeting errors and distributional design can slow measured impacts</cite> <cite id="ec5b5395-1">whereas adequate hours and reliability accelerate electrification benefits</cite>. 
- Contextual constraints: <cite id="6a262056-3">Without extension, inputs, and markets, agriculture-linked programs can be lumpy or slow</cite> <cite id="ec5b5395-0">and some electrification studies show no income effects absent complementary reforms</cite>.

Practical implications
- To maximize speed, combine fast-acting liquidity with constraint relief: <cite id="6a262056-3">adequate, predictable, and seasonally timed transfers</cite> plus <cite id="e8844cf6-2">last-mile roads</cite> and <cite id="ec5b5395-3">reliable electricity</cite> to convert cash into productivity. 
- For agriculture-led strategies, pair cash or input subsidies with extension and market linkages to accelerate and stabilize gains: <cite id="e8844cf6-1">subsidy diversion toward non-food crops quickly lifts rural incomes</cite> <cite id="6a262056-3">but sustained exit requires enabling investments and information services</cite>. 
- Avoid designs that are lumpy or ill-timed: <cite id="6a262056-1">uneven Village Cash Transfer effects in Indonesia highlight the need for deeper targeting to the ultra-poor</cite> <cite id="6a262056-3">and predictable disbursements aligned with agricultural cycles</cite>.

Bottom line
- The fastest and most consistently measurable rural poverty reductions come from cash-based social protection and rural electrification, followed closely by feeder road investments and well-designed agricultural input/asset programs; microfinance alone tends to be slower and more heterogeneous. <cite id="6a262056-0">Cash transfers reduce monetary poverty quickly with local multipliers</cite> <cite id="6a262056-4">and demonstrable gains within two years</cite>, while <cite id="ec5b5395-1">electrification boosts consumption and poverty-exit probabilities within a year</cite> and <cite id="e8844cf6-2">rural roads deliver large pro-poor returns over 1–3 years via mobility</cite>. Speed advantages arise from direct liquidity, last-mile constraint relief, and reliable, predictable service delivery that convert assistance into immediate welfare and income gains. <cite id="6a262056-3">Program adequacy, predictability, and alignment with agricultural cycles are critical to shortening the time path</cite>, and <cite id="ec5b5395-3">reliability of power roughly doubles income gains</cite>. Where agriculture-oriented supports are paired with markets and extension, rural subsidy reforms can also produce rapid income and poverty declines, especially in rural settings. <cite id="e8844cf6-1">Simulations show rural poverty falling by several percentage points within a year when subsidies are diverted to non-food crops</cite>.

Title: Strategies for Reducing Rural Poverty in Developing Countries
Snippet: Rural poverty in developing countries comes in various forms. Food insecurity, discrimination, human rights violations, inadequate health care, and social protection are just some of the manifestations of poverty that affect the rural population. However, the most severe form of poverty is the lack of access to food for the most vulnerable segments of the population. Several strategic approaches to rural poverty reduction have been developed at the international level and have been implemented specifically in developing countries. These strategies focus on agriculture as the dominant economic activity in rural areas. In addition, the strategies aim to strengthen local rural communities while adhering to the principles of environmental, economic, and social sustainability.
</snippet>

The diversion subsidy of 12. 35 percent can reduce poverty by 1. 61 percent of total poor house holds in the city, and 2. 18 percent in rural area. Furthermore, subsidy is the most effective way to alleviate the rural poverty, as Ravallion and Datt (1999) argued that the growth in the agricultural sector is the most efficient way in reducing income in equality and the poverty. Arndt, et.al (1998) also support this argument with his empirical findings that the development of the agricultural sector can reduce poverty. 

Institute of Bogor Agricultural carried out empirical research in 2002, and found that the Agriculture Based Development (ABD) model may spur higher economic growth.
